9.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.1.b:
SCFE is the hip disease every orthopaedic surgeon meets, and the one most often missed.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is SCFE?"
- "The **neck slips anteriorly and superiorly** off the epiphysis, through the physis."
- "It is a disease of the **obese adolescent**, 10–16 years, boys twice as often."
- "Mild slips are cheap to fix; missed slips become severe."

### Definition
The name describes what the eye sees, not what really moves.
- **Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)**: the capital epiphysis slips off the neck at the **physis**
- The head looks displaced **posteriorly and inferiorly**
[[FIG: Fig 9.1 · 9.1
- But the head stays in the acetabulum
- So the **neck** really moves: **anteriorly and superiorly**, and it rotates externally

#### A Misnomer
- The epiphysis never leaves the socket, so "slipped epiphysis" is a misnomer
- Its old name is **adolescent coxa vara**: head below, neck above, shaft adducted
- Developmental and congenital coxa vara → 10 Coxa Vara

### Epidemiology
Picture the patient before the film: a heavy boy at his growth spurt.

| Feature | Typical value |
|---|---|
| Age | **10–16** years; 78% in the rapid growth phase |
| Sex | boys **2×** girls |
| Build | **obese**; sometimes tall |
| Bilateral | ≈**25%** (17–50%) |
| Second slip | usually within **12–18 months** |

- Bilaterality is quoted as 25–40% (Campbell); 25% is the safe exam figure (Miller)
- Boys mature about 2 years later, so they stay at risk longer
- Endocrine and renal cases are under **10%**, so most bilateral slips are **obese**

MEMORY HOOK — the heavy teenager
- SCFE is a heavy teenager sliding off a stool: weight from above, a soft physis below, and a growth spurt shaking the stool.

9.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.2.b:
A weak physis meets a shear force it cannot resist; everything else explains one of the two.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why does the physis slip?"
- "A **weak physis** (growth spurt, hormones, vitamin D) meets **shear** (obesity, retroversion)."
- "It slips through the **hypertrophic zone**."
- "Once the posterior slope passes **15°**, less force slips it further: a vicious circle."

### The Weak Physis
The physis is weakest exactly when the adolescent grows fastest.

#### Slip Zone
- SCFE slips through the **hypertrophic zone** (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 9.2 · 9.2
- There cells are large and many, and the matrix is scant
- Strength lies in the matrix, so this zone is the weakest

| Separation | Zone |
|---|---|
| **SCFE** | hypertrophic (maturation) zone |
| Traumatic (Salter–Harris I) | zone of provisional calcification |

#### Loss of Protective Mechanisms
| Protector | What happens before maturity |
|---|---|
| **Perichondral ring of La Croix** | thins, losing its periosteal collar |
| **Concavo-convex** epiphysis–metaphysis fit | flattens |
| **Mammillary processes** (micro-interlocks) | loosen |
| Physis | widens, as growth hormone drives proliferation |

- **Vitamin D deficiency** and hormonal imbalance widen the physis
- A widened physis is held only by cartilage, so it slides easily

### Mechanical Causes
These factors turn body weight into shear across the plate.
| Factor | How it adds shear |
|---|---|
| **Obesity** (the greatest risk) | load, and vitamin D deficiency |
| **Tall stature** | load, and more growth hormone |
| **Coxa vara** | vertical physis: weight becomes shear |
| **Femoral retroversion** | physis faces the anteroposterior shear |

#### Acetabular Retroversion
- Early belief: a **deep acetabulum** overcovered the head; this is wrong
- Most cases show a **retroverted acetabulum**, overcovering the head anteriorly
[[FIG: Fig 9.3 · 9.2
- Normal acetabular and femoral anteversion are both about **15°**

### Endocrine and Renal Causes
Hormones decide how wide and how long the physis stays open.

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Hypothyroidism** | the commonest hormonal cause; poor cartilage calcification |
| Growth hormone excess | stimulates the proliferative zone |
| **Hypogonadism** | delays physeal closure |
| Hyperparathyroidism | rare; thick, mitotic physis |
| **Renal osteodystrophy** | slip in the metaphyseal **spongiosa**, not cartilage |

- All hormonal causes together are only ≈**5%** of SCFE (Handbook)
- Hypothyroidism accounts for ≈**40%** of the hormonal group
- Endocrine and renal slips are typically **bilateral**

#### Atypical Age
- A child younger than **10** years needs an endocrine work-up (Miller)
- Onset after **16** years suggests hypogonadism
- Radiotherapy and **Down syndrome** are also associated

MEMORY HOOK — the wrong birthday
- A slip at the wrong birthday (under 10 or over 16) is an endocrine slip until the blood tests say otherwise.

### Posterior Slope Angle
This angle measures how far the physis already leans backwards.
- **Posterior slope angle (PSA)**: the physis plane against the perpendicular to the neck axis, on the lateral view
[[FIG: Fig 9.4 · 9.2
- Above **15°**, energy to failure **halves** with every 5° more (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- So a 20° physis slips with half the force of a 15° one
- Beyond **50°**, almost no force is needed

### The Vicious Circle
Once started, each step makes the next easier.
- Retroversion plus shear → slip → less force needed → more slip
[[FIG: Fig 9.5 · 9.2
- Slip → coxa vara → raised joint load → limp → more shear
- So fix the slip while it is mild: progression accelerates

9.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.3.b:
The slip leaves a predictable deformity, and every later problem comes from it.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what deformity does SCFE leave?"
- "Varus, extension and external rotation of the head–neck relation."
- "An **anterior metaphyseal bump**: the cam that wears the hip."
- "A short neck and a high trochanter: weak abductors."

### Direction and Degree of Slip
The epiphysis tilts back and down as the slip grows.
- Mild, moderate and severe slips differ in the **posterior tilt** of the head
[[FIG: Fig 9.6 · 9.3
- The prominent anterior neck strikes the acetabulum in flexion and IR (internal rotation)
- So motion is blocked by **impingement**, not by pain alone

### Remodelling and Callus
A chronic slip heals in its wrong place.
- In a chronic slip, the posterior neck forms **callus**, and the anterior edge rounds off
[[FIG: Fig 9.7 · 9.3
- The callus fills the angle under the tilted head
- It makes reduction impossible without cutting it away

### Retinacular Blood Supply
SCFE threatens the same vessels that the hip operations try to save; hip blood supply → 01 Approach.
- The **posterosuperior retinacular vessels** run up the neck to the epiphysis
[[FIG: Fig 9.8 · 9.3
- They come from the deep branch of the **medial circumflex femoral artery (MFCA)**
- The retinaculum is the periosteum of the neck
- Forceful reduction **stretches** these vessels against the callus → AVN (avascular necrosis)

9.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.4.b:
Three separate classifications answer three separate questions; mixing them is the classic viva error.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you classify SCFE?"
- "**Clinical**: Loder stable or unstable, by weight bearing; it predicts AVN."
- "**Chronological**: pre-slip, acute, chronic, acute-on-chronic."
- "**Radiological**: Southwick slip angle or displacement: mild, moderate, severe."

| Classification | Based on | Example answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Clinical (Loder)** | ability to bear weight | unstable |
| **Chronological** | history and time | acute-on-chronic |
| **Radiological** | slip angle or displacement | severe |

- Combine all three: "acute-on-chronic, severe, unstable SCFE"
- Never answer "Loder, acute and chronic" as if it were one scheme

### Loder Stability Classification
Stability, not duration, predicts the dreaded complication.

| Type | Definition | AVN (Campbell) |
|---|---|---|
| **Stable** | walks, with or without crutches | **0%** |
| **Unstable** | cannot walk at all, even with crutches | **47%** |

- Satisfactory results: **96%** of stable slips, **47%** of unstable ones
- Acute is not unstable: a child who fell yesterday and walks is acute but stable

MEMORY HOOK — the crutch test
- Give the child crutches: if he walks, the slip is stable; if he cannot take a step even with crutches, the head is in danger (47% AVN).

#### Limits of the Loder Definition
- Clinical stability does not match **intraoperative instability**, the true stability
[[FIG: Fig 9.9 · 9.4
- Loder criteria: sensitivity **39%**, specificity **76%** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

#### Other Signs of Instability
| Sign | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Effusion** on ultrasound or MRI | acute tear |
| Head **reduces** with gentle IR under the image | unstable |
| Cannot bear weight **+** effusion | caught **100%** of unstable slips |

- So an open physis may be unstable even in a walking child

### Chronological Classification
Duration describes the story but carries little prognostic value.

| Type | History | Radiograph |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-slip** | pain, no deformity | physis widened, irregular |
| **Acute** | sudden, under **3 weeks** | sharp edges, no remodelling |
| **Chronic** | gradual, over 3 weeks | rounded edges, posterior callus |
| **Acute-on-chronic** | long mild pain, sudden worsening | head beyond the remodelled neck |

- Chronic slips are the majority, ≈**60%** (Handbook)
[[FIG: Fig 9.10 · 9.4
- Acute slips are ≈10%; the rest are acute-on-chronic
- Pre-slip: MRI shows **oedema** around the physis
- The Handbook also calls a painful hip with a contralateral slip pre-slip

### Southwick Slip Angle
This is the grading examiners mean by "how severe is the slip?".
- Measured on the **frog-lateral** view: physis line, its perpendicular, and the shaft axis
[[FIG: Fig 9.11 · 9.4
- The **head–shaft angle** is the angle between the perpendicular and the shaft
[[FIG: Fig 9.12 · 9.4
- Grade by the **difference** from the normal side
- Normal is under **12–15°** on the lateral view
- With bilateral slips, compare with reference values: **145°** AP (anteroposterior) and **10°** lateral (Handbook)

| Grade | Slip angle difference (Campbell) |
|---|---|
| **Mild** (I) | ≤**30°** |
| **Moderate** (II) | **30–60°** |
| **Severe** (III) | >**60°** |

PITFALL — severe from 50° or from 60°?
- The Handbook grades severe above **50°**; Campbell and the lecture's main scale use **60°**
- Say → "**mild ≤30°, moderate 30–60°, severe >60° (Southwick, frog-lateral)**"

### Displacement Grading
Older grading uses how far the neck has moved on the head.
- Neck displacement as a fraction of the head diameter
[[FIG: Fig 9.13 · 9.4
- Mild: under **⅓** · moderate: ⅓–½
- Severe: over **½** of the head width

9.5.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.5.b:
The story is a limp and knee pain; the sign is a hip that will not rotate inwards.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does SCFE present?"
- "A heavy adolescent with a **limp** and **knee pain**."
- "**Limited internal rotation**, external rotation deformity, shortening."
- "**Drehmann sign**: the hip rolls into external rotation as it flexes."

### Symptoms
Pain often points to the wrong joint.
- **Knee pain** is the commonest complaint, in about half the children
- The hip capsule and medial knee share the **obturator nerve**
- Pain may be absent: a **painless limp** is still SCFE until disproved

PITFALL — the knee MRI
- A missed SCFE often has a knee MRI, then a meniscal "tear", then arthroscopy is advised
- Say → "**knee pain in an adolescent: examine the hip, and X-ray it if internal rotation is limited**"

### Signs
Each sign follows from the neck moving forward and up.

| Sign | Cause |
|---|---|
| **External rotation** of the limb | head posterior, neck anterior |
| **Limited internal rotation** | anterior neck impinges on the rim |
| Limited abduction and flexion | superior neck impinges; capsule tight |
| **Shortening** | neck migrates upward |
| **Trendelenburg** gait | high trochanter slackens abductors |
| Genu valgum | the tilt adducts the femur |

- Bilateral slips walk with a **waddling** gait
[[FIG: Fig 9.14 · 9.5
- Unstable slips cannot bear weight and lie in external rotation
- Thigh atrophy and an outward foot progression angle mark a chronic slip

#### Drehmann Sign
- Flex the supine hip to **90°**: it rolls into obligatory **external rotation**
- Flexion with IR jams the anterior neck against the rim, so the hip escapes into ER (external rotation)
- It is also positive in Perthes disease → 05 Perthes Pathology

MEMORY HOOK — the shy knee
- In SCFE the knee does the talking and the hip stays quiet: always look one joint up.

9.6.l: Pediatric Hip — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
9.6.b:
Two views diagnose almost every slip; one view misses the mild ones.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what X-rays, and what signs?"
- "**AP pelvis plus frog-lateral** of both hips; never the AP alone."
- "AP: widened physis, **Klein line** fails, low epiphysis, **blanch sign**."
- "Lateral: posterior tilt, measured by the **Southwick angle**."

### Radiographic Views
The slip is posterior, so it shows best side-on.
- **AP pelvis** shows both hips for comparison
- **Frog-lateral** is the most important view: a mild slip may hide on the AP
[[FIG: Fig 9.15 · 9.6
- An unstable slip gets a **cross-table lateral**, not a frog view

### Signs on the Anteroposterior View
Each sign is the shadow of a head tilted back and down.

#### Physeal Widening
- The first sign is a **widened, irregular physis** (epiphysiolysis)
[[FIG: Fig 9.16 · 9.6
- Normally the physis is narrow and the epiphysis interlocks with the neck

#### Klein Line and Trethowan Sign
- **Klein line**: drawn along the superior neck, it should cut part of the epiphysis
[[FIG: Fig 9.17 · 9.6
- **Trethowan sign**: the line misses the epiphysis, or cuts less than the other side
[[FIG: Fig 9.18 · 9.6
- A line that still crosses does not exclude a slip: **compare sides**
[[FIG: Fig 9.19 · 9.6
- A ≥**2 mm** side difference raises sensitivity from 40% to ≈80% (Campbell)

#### Reduced Epiphyseal Height
- The tilted epiphysis looks **shorter** than the other side
[[FIG: Fig 9.20 · 9.6
- Its thin anterior part now faces upward

#### Metaphyseal Blanch Sign of Steel
- A **crescent of double density** over the proximal metaphysis
[[FIG: Fig 9.21 · 9.6
- The posteriorly slipped epiphysis overlaps the neck on the AP view

#### Capener Triangular Sign
- Normally the posterior acetabular wall overlaps the **inferomedial neck**, forming a dense triangle
[[FIG: Fig 9.22 · 9.6
- In SCFE the neck moves up and out, so the **triangle disappears**
[[FIG: Fig 9.23 · 9.6

| Sign | View | Finding in SCFE |
|---|---|---|
| Physis | AP and lateral | widened, irregular |
| **Klein line** (Trethowan) | AP | misses the epiphysis, or cuts less |
| Epiphyseal height | AP | reduced |
| **Blanch sign of Steel** | AP | metaphyseal double density |
| **Capener triangle** | AP | lost |
| **Southwick angle** | frog-lateral | above the normal 12–15° |

MEMORY HOOK — the ice cream
- The epiphysis is ice cream slipping off its cone: from the front it looks shorter (low height), blurs the cone (blanch) and falls below the cone's edge line (Klein).

### Cross-Sectional and Other Imaging
Advanced imaging answers questions the plain film cannot.

#### Computed Tomography

9.7.b:
Treatment arrests the slip first, then restores the anatomy, without killing the head.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat SCFE?"
- "Stable mild: **in situ pinning**, one central screw, no reduction."
- "Unstable: **urgent** fixation, gentle positional reduction, **capsular decompression**."
- "Severe or unpinnable: **modified Dunn** in expert hands."

### Aims of Treatment
Two aims, in this order.
- First, **arrest progression**: fix the slip while it is mild
- Second, **restore anatomy**: less impingement, less arthritis
- A perfect film with a dead head is a failure

### Treatment Algorithm
Decide by stability first, then by severity.
[[FIG: Fig 9.30 · 9.7

| Slip | Treatment (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
|---|---|
| Unstable | urgent fixation + capsular decompression |
| Stable mild | in situ pinning |
| Stable moderate | in situ pinning + neck osteoplasty |
| Severe or unpinnable | open reduction (modified Dunn) |

- Bed rest, traction and closed reduction in a spica are abandoned: ineffective
- Never manipulate a **chronic** slip: the callus blocks it and the vessels tear

### In Situ Pinning
Pinning is the workhorse: quick, cheap and safe when done right.

#### Indications
- All stable slips, and most unstable ones, are fixed **in situ**
- It is also used for a pre-slip and for prophylaxis of the other hip
- Mild slips: pinning alone; moderate: pinning plus an add-on

#### Epiphysiodesis or Physeal-Sparing Pinning
- Both arrest the slip; they differ in whether the physis keeps growing
[[FIG: Fig 9.31 · 9.7
- **Epiphysiodesis**: screw threads cross the physis, so growth stops
[[FIG: Fig 9.32 · 9.7

| | Epiphysiodesis | Physeal sparing |
|---|---|---|
| Across the physis | threads | smooth shank |
| Growth | arrested | continues |
| Cam remodelling | prevented | allowed |
| Neck | short, less offset | length kept |
| ATD (articulotrochanteric distance) | falls | kept |
| Suits | little growth left | young child |

#### Effect of Physeal Fusion
- The proximal femoral physis grows ≈**3 mm** a year (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- So fusion at 10 years, with 6 years left, costs ≈**1.8 cm**
- Fusion shortens the neck and raises the trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 9.33 · 9.7
- The result copies the untreated slip: short lever arm, high joint load
[[FIG: Fig 9.34 · 9.7

MEMORY HOOK — the parking brake

#### Physeal-Sparing Devices
- **Hansson** hook pin: a smooth rod whose inner hook interlocks in the epiphysis
[[FIG: Fig 9.35 · 9.7
- Smooth metal crossing once does not fuse the physis; repeated drilling does
- **K-wires**, bent on the lateral cortex, are a cheap substitute
[[FIG: Fig 9.36 · 9.7
- Telescoping screws and the **AO SCFE screw** carry short threads in the epiphysis
[[FIG: Fig 9.37 · 9.7
- Three **2 mm** wires matched one 6.5 mm screw in strength (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 9.38 · 9.7
- The family must accept follow-up and longer wires as the child grows
[[FIG: Fig 9.39 · 9.7

#### Choosing the Concept
- **Young** child, much growth left: physeal sparing
- Girls usually stop growing near 14 years: a 12-year-old girl gets fusion
- Follow every screw until the physis **fuses**: growth past a screw re-slips
[[FIG: Fig 9.40 · 9.7

#### Screw Choice
- One cannulated **6.5–7 mm** screw is enough
- **Fully threaded**: no compression is wanted, and it comes out easily
[[FIG: Fig 9.41 · 9.7
- A partially threaded screw has no back-cutting threads, so removal is hard
- A **washer** is a mistake: compression is not the aim

#### Number of Screws
- **One** central screw: the epiphysis has no room for two
[[FIG: Fig 9.42 · 9.7
- A second screw adds penetration risk without proven strength
- A very unstable slip may take a second screw below the first

| Rule | Target |
|---|---|

| Direction | **perpendicular** to the physis |
| Threads | at least **5** across the physis |
| Tip | no closer than **4–5 mm** to subchondral bone (Campbell) |

- Avoid the **anterosuperior** quadrant: highest penetration (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 9.43 · 9.7

#### Entry Point
- The head sits posterior, so entry is **anterior** on the neck, never lateral
[[FIG: Fig 9.44 · 9.7

[[FIG: Fig 9.45 · 9.7
- A lateral entry exits the anterior epiphysis: penetration
[[FIG: Fig 9.46 · 9.7
- Lay one wire for the AP line and one for the lateral; they cross **anterolaterally**
[[FIG: Fig 9.47 · 9.7
- In a severe slip the perpendicular path meets the **femoral vessels**: unpinnable

| Slip | Entry |
|---|---|
| Mild | anterolateral neck |
| Severe | anterior, almost anteromedial |
| Very severe | through the femoral nerve: not pinnable |

[[FIG: Fig 9.48 · 9.7

[[FIG: Fig 9.49 · 9.7

| Slip | Weight bearing (Campbell) |
|---|---|
| Stable | as tolerated, crutches **2–3 weeks** |
| Unstable | partial, **6–8 weeks** |

- Warn the family about the **other hip**: come back at the first pain

Pinning stops the slip but leaves the bump; a moderate slip needs both.
- A moderate slip has a clear anterior **bump**: a cam
- Add **neck osteoplasty** to restore the head–neck offset
[[FIG: Fig 9.50 · 9.7
- Routes: arthroscopic, limited anterior arthrotomy, or surgical dislocation
- The lecturer pins, then shaves through a short anterior approach
[[FIG: Fig 9.51 · 9.7
- Detach the rectus femoris, open the capsule, and trim the bump
[[FIG: Fig 9.52 · 9.7
- The offset is restored and kept; the labrum is spared
[[FIG: Fig 9.53 · 9.7

#### Bone Peg Epiphysiodesis
- **Heyman–Herndon**: a strut graft through an anterior neck tunnel fuses the physis
[[FIG: Fig 9.54 · 9.7
- Osteoplasty can be done through the same window
- Against screws: longer surgery, blood loss, wound problems, failed fusion, AVN risk

### Unstable Slip
An unstable slip behaves like a femoral neck fracture, not cold surgery.
- Operate **urgently**: ideally within **24 hours**
[[FIG: Fig 9.55 · 9.7
- Accept the reduction that comes with **positioning** on the table
- Never manipulate forcefully: it is strongly linked to **AVN**

#### Capsular Decompression
- **Capsulotomy** or aspiration releases the tamponade
- Hip pressure in an unstable slip is **double** the normal side

#### Timing and Reduction
- Some advise waiting **7 days** if the first 24 hours are missed: the "unsafe window"
- A gentle **Leadbetter** manoeuvre has advocates; force has none
- Acute-on-chronic: reduce only back to the chronic remodelled position

### Modified Dunn Procedure
This open reduction corrects the deformity at its apex while protecting the retinacular flap.

#### Rationale
- A chronic slip has posterior **callus**
[[FIG: Fig 9.56 · 9.7
- Reducing over it stretches the posterosuperior retinacular vessels → AVN
[[FIG: Fig 9.57 · 9.7
- Removing the callus and shortening the neck lets the head return slack
- Correction is at the **CORA**, the centre of rotation of angulation, so it is anatomical

#### Indications
- **Severe** slips: Southwick angle over **60°**
- Any slip that **CT** shows to be **unpinnable**, even under 60°
- Bern centres extend it to moderate and unstable slips: evidence is still debated

#### Surgical Anatomy
- The deep branch of the **MFCA** runs deep to the external rotators
[[FIG: Fig 9.58 · 9.7
- Its main branch lies just above and behind the **lesser trochanter**
[[FIG: Fig 9.59 · 9.7
- The trochanteric osteotomy stays **superficial to the piriformis**
[[FIG: Fig 9.60 · 9.7
- So piriformis and rotators stay on the stable trochanter, guarding the vessels
[[FIG: Fig 9.61 · 9.7

#### Approach and Exposure
- **Lateral decubitus**, the leg free in a sterile bag
[[FIG: Fig 9.62 · 9.7
- Straight lateral incision; the Gibson interval behind the gluteus maximus
[[FIG: Fig 9.63 · 9.7
- Open the trochanteric bursa
[[FIG: Fig 9.64 · 9.7
- **Trochanteric flip** osteotomy: a digastric flap of gluteus medius and vastus lateralis
- Keep the fragment under **1.5 cm** thick (Campbell)
- **Z-shaped capsulotomy**, staying anterior to the lesser trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 9.65 · 9.7

#### Reduction Steps
- An unstable head is **pinned with wires** before dislocation
[[FIG: Fig 9.66 · 9.7
- Dislocate anteriorly; cut the ligamentum teres
[[FIG: Fig 9.67 · 9.7
- Raise the **retinacular flap** subperiosteally, after trimming the stable trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 9.68 · 9.7
- Free the epiphysis from the neck with a curved osteotome
[[FIG: Fig 9.69 · 9.7
- Remove **callus**, curette the physis, and round the neck stump
[[FIG: Fig 9.70 · 9.7
- Reduce under vision; stop if the retinaculum tightens
[[FIG: Fig 9.71 · 9.7
- Fix with **threaded wires** through the fovea, or smooth wires bent laterally
[[FIG: Fig 9.72 · 9.7
- Fix the trochanter with 2–3 screws
[[FIG: Fig 9.73 · 9.7
- Check for no varus, valgus or retroversion under the image

#### Testing Head Perfusion
- Drill a **2 mm** hole in the head before dislocation
[[FIG: Fig 9.74 · 9.7
- Fresh **bleeding** means the head is alive
[[FIG: Fig 9.75 · 9.7
- Finger pressure on the retinaculum stops the flow; release restores it
[[FIG: Fig 9.76 · 9.7
- That proves **arterial** flow, not venous congestion
[[FIG: Fig 9.77 · 9.7

#### Cases
- An 11-year-old boy with a severe slip: anatomical reduction
[[FIG: Fig 9.78 · 9.7
- A 13-year-old boy, unpinnable on CT, healed with good offset
[[FIG: Fig 9.79 · 9.7
- Another 13-year-old had no perpendicular entry, but good circulation
[[FIG: Fig 9.80 · 9.7

#### Results
- In good hands, AVN after modified Dunn was **7%** (Campbell)
- Wider series report AVN approaching **25%** (Miller)
- Late presentation brings softened heads and eroded cartilage
[[FIG: Fig 9.81 · 9.7
- Pinning remains the standard; the Dunn belongs to experienced centres

### Realignment Osteotomies
When the physis has closed on a deformity, the osteotomy chooses between safety and correction.
[[FIG: Fig 9.82 · 9.7

| Site | Correction | AVN risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Neck, near the physis** (cuneiform, Dunn) | complete | high |
| **Base of neck** (Kramer) | partial | lower |
| **Intertrochanteric** (Imhäuser, Southwick) | compensatory | lowest |

- **Cuneiform** neck osteotomy: AVN and arthritis each ≈**37%** (Miller)
- **Southwick** osteotomy at the lesser trochanter corrects varus, extension and rotation
- **Imhäuser** osteotomy flexes the shaft mainly; it also corrects varus and ER
[[FIG: Fig 9.83 · 9.7
- **Kramer** base-of-neck wedge lies distal to the retinacular vessels
[[FIG: Fig 9.84 · 9.7
- Compensatory osteotomies leave a zigzag deformity, so impingement persists

### Contralateral Prophylactic Pinning
The other hip slips often, but pinning a normal hip has its own price.
- A contralateral slip follows in **20–40%** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 9.85 · 9.7
- Prophylactic pinning remains **controversial**: AVN, fracture and penetration can wreck a normal hip
[[FIG: Fig 9.86 · 9.7
- Not pinned? Warn the family to return at the first pain

| Pin the other hip when (Campbell) |
|---|
| **young**: girls under 10, boys under 12 |
| **endocrine** or renal disease

The worst complications are made at surgery, so know how each one arises.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the complications of SCFE?"
- "**AVN**: the unstable slip and forceful reduction."
- "**Chondrolysis**: joint space under 3 mm, usually from screw penetration."
- "**FAI and arthritis**: the residual cam, even after mild slips."

### Osteonecrosis
AVN follows injury to the retinacular vessels.
[[FIG: Fig 9.88 · 9.8

#### Risk Factors
- **Instability** is the best predictor: up to **50%** of unstable slips (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 9.89–9.90 · 9.8
- Forceful manipulation, delayed fixation and **tamponade** add to it
- **Superolateral** screws injure the lateral epiphyseal vessels
- **Anterior physeal separation** on the frog view predicts AVN
[[FIG: Fig 9.91 · 9.8
- It is rare in chronic stable slips

#### Management
- **Non-weight bearing** and range-of-motion exercises
- No core decompression: the screw track already drilled the head

### Chondrolysis
Cartilage loss stiffens a young hip and resists every treatment.
- Joint space under **3 mm** (normal 4–6 mm), with lost motion (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 9.92 · 9.8
- **Persistent pin penetration** is the commonest cited cause
- Transient penetration, withdrawn at once, does no harm

#### Treatment
- Anti-inflammatory drugs, physiotherapy, arthroscopy and capsulectomy help little
- Persistent narrowing may end in arthrodesis or arthroplasty

### Other Complications
Hardware and growth make up the rest.
- **Continued slipping** occurs in up to **2%** after in situ pinning (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 9.93 · 9.8
- **Subtrochanteric fracture** follows extra drill holes and stress risers
- **Leg-length discrepancy** follows epiphysiodesis in a young child
- The other hip may slip later

### Long-Term Outcome
Any degree of slip leaves its mark.
- Severe deformity, osteonecrosis and instability bring poor long-term results
[[FIG: Fig 9.94 · 9.9
- Mild and moderate slips do far better
- Scandinavian follow-up over 25–35 years still showed more arthritis
[[FIG: Fig 9.95 · 9.9
- Clinical impingement was found in **32–38%** of young adults after SCFE (Campbell)

### Femoroacetabular Impingement
SCFE is the severest form of cam impingement.
- The anterior metaphysis becomes a **cam**, jamming into the labrum in flexion
[[FIG: Fig 9.96 · 9.9
- Retroversion adds a **pincer** effect, even if the cam is small
[[FIG: Fig 9.97 · 9.9
- A long-standing severe slip may leave a **pistol-grip** deformity

| Type | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Cam** | anterior neck bump |
| **Pincer** | retroverted femur and acetabulum |
| **Instability** | double-bubble acetabulum in severe old slips |

#### Alpha Angle
- **Alpha angle**: head centre to neck axis, against head centre to where the head leaves its circle
[[FIG: Fig 9.98 · 9.9
- Normal is under **55°** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 9.99 · 9.9
- The anterior bump best predicts long-term arthritis
- So moderate slips with a high alpha angle get an osteoplasty

#### Double-Bubble Acetabulum
- A long-standing severe slip moulds **two concavities** in the acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 9.100 · 9.9
- After reduction, the head sits on the ridge: the hip is **unstable**
[[FIG: Fig 9.101 · 9.9
- A spica is the only answer, and very hard in an obese child

### Pathomechanics of Arthritis
The deformity overloads the hip even without a cam.
- The neck migrates up, so the **trochanter rides high**
[[FIG: Fig 9.102 · 9.9
- Abductors slacken and their lever arm shortens
- Moment = force × lever arm, so the abductor force must rise
- That raises the **joint reaction force** → early wear

#### Same Mechanics After Fusion
- Physeal fusion after a screw recreates this short-neck mechanics
